linkedin.title: This Week in Finance & Tech
linkedin.body:
Microsoft is reportedly offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees. This move affects over a quarter of their global workforce and is aimed at cutting costs as the company shifts its focus toward AI integration.

In California, Mark Zuckerberg has reached a deal with Meta that keeps him in the state. The company’s board was concerned that his potential departure over a proposed wealth tax could derail their AI goals. A new stock agreement has been put in place to help him manage the financial impact if that tax measure becomes law.

In legal news, a US judge has ordered Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 regarding his 10 billion dollar lawsuit against the BBC. If he does not cooperate with the discovery process, the judge has threatened to dismiss the case entirely.

On the policy front, UK Chancellor Rachel Reeves has unveiled her first budget. It includes a 100 pound credit for energy bills and a new tax on banks, aimed at addressing the cost of living while managing economic uncertainty.

Finally, Apple users have a new update. iOS 27.2 is now rolling out, bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo. The update also adds an Edge Light feature designed to brighten faces during video calls.

instagram.title: Christine Lagarde resigns early as ECB President

slides.headline: Christine Lagarde resigns early as ECB President
slides.subtitle: She leaves her post months ahead of schedule

slides.explanation: The European Central Bank manages the currency for twenty countries in the eurozone. Her departure impacts financial policy for millions of people.

slides.headline: Freedom to speak on non-monetary policy
slides.explanation: Lagarde says she wants more freedom to speak, which is fueling rumors about her potential run in the upcoming French presidential election.
This news is verified by four independent outlets, including France 24 and the Guardian.

slides.subtitle: Read the full analysis on Headlinne.

instagram.caption:
Christine Lagarde is stepping down as President of the European Central Bank.

She is leaving her post several months early to gain more freedom to discuss topics outside of monetary policy.

Her exit is already sparking intense speculation about her future. With a presidential election approaching in France, many are wondering if she plans to enter the race.

This move marks a significant shift for one of the most powerful financial institutions in the world. We are watching closely to see what she says next.

story.title: ECB President Lagarde steps down in order to speak out
story.summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down from her post several months early, in order to have more "freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy." The comments will fuel speculation about her future plans, ahead of a presidential election in her native France. The resignation also sparks a succession race, as Europe faces a turbulent fiscal future. Also in the show - oil giant TotalEnergies reports record profits as the EU warns on household energy bills.

story_card.caption:
